q: Which statement about a Python list is correct?
options: All of its items must have the same type, or Python refuses the list
It cannot be changed once it has been created, like a string
Python keeps its items in sorted order by itself as they are added
It keeps its items in order, may mix types, and can be changed in place
why: A list is an ordered value whose items may be of different types, and unlike a string or a tuple it can be changed in the same object.

q: What does len() count when it is given a list that holds another list?
options: Every value, including those inside the inner list
The characters in the printed text of the list
The outer items; an inner list counts as one
The highest index that is in use in the list
why: len() returns the number of items of the list it is given, and an inner list is a single item of the outer one.

q: What makes a value a list when it is written in a program?
options: Items separated by commas between round brackets
Items separated by commas between square brackets
Items separated by commas between curly braces
Items separated by spaces after the word list
why: A list is written between square brackets; round brackets make a tuple and curly braces a set or a dictionary.

q: What does this program print?
code:
data = [['cat', 'bat'], [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]]
print(data[1][4], len(data))
why: data[1] is the second inner list, its index 4 is the fifth item 50, and the outer list holds two items.

q: Why can len(spam) be 4 while the last valid index of spam is 3?
options: len() counts one item too many
len() counts the items, and indexes start at 0
The last index is always len minus two
Python reserves the last position for a marker
why: len() returns the number of items and indexes count from 0, so the last index is one less than the length.

q: What does this program print?
code:
spam = ['a', ['b', 'c'], 'd']
print(len(spam), len(spam[1]), len([]))
why: The outer list has three items, the inner list two, and the empty list none.

q: What is the difference between an index and a slice?
options: An index gives a new list, a slice gives one item of the list
Both give one item, but a slice counts from the end of the list
A slice changes the list in place, while an index only reads it
An index gives one item, a slice gives a new list of a run of items
why: An index picks one item of a list and a slice picks a run of items, which comes back as a new list.

q: What does the index -1 pick out of a list?
options: The last item
The first item
Nothing, since negative indexes do not exist
The whole list read backwards
why: A negative index counts from the end, so spam[-1] is the last item.

q: What does this program print?
options: IndexError
bat IndexError
bat elephant
rat elephant
why: spam[-3] is 'bat', but spam[4] is out of range, and the exception stops the print call before it prints anything.

q: Why does spam[1:3] not include the item at index 3?
options: Slices always drop the last item of the list they cut
A slice stops before its end index
The second number is a length, so it takes three items
A four-item list has no index 3, so the slice stops early
why: A slice runs up to but not including the end index.

q: What does this program print?
code:
spam = ['cat', 'bat', 'rat', 'elephant']
print(spam[1:10], spam[::2], spam[-2:])
options: IndexError
['bat', 'rat', 'elephant'] ['bat', 'elephant'] ['rat', 'elephant']
['bat', 'rat', 'elephant'] ['cat', 'rat'] ['rat', 'elephant']
['bat', 'rat'] ['cat', 'rat'] ['rat', 'elephant']
why: A slice past the end does not raise, a step of 2 takes every second item from the start, and -2 starts two items from the end.

q: Which of these can be done to a list but not to a string or a tuple?
options: Read an item by its index
Ask for its length with len()
Cut a run of items out with a slice
Replace one item inside the same object
why: Unlike a string or a tuple, a list can be changed in the same object, by adding, replacing and removing items.

q: Which statement puts a new value at the end of the list spam?
options: spam.add(value)
spam.insert(value)
spam[len(spam)] = value
spam.append(value)
why: append() adds its argument at the end; insert() needs an index first, and assigning to an index that does not exist raises IndexError.

q: What does append() return?
options: The new list, with the item added at its end
None, after adding the item to the list
The item that was added, so it can be reused
The new length of the list after the addition
why: A method that changes a mutable object returns None, so append() changes the list and gives back nothing useful.

q: What does this program print?
code:
spam = ['cat', 'dog']
result = spam.append('moose')
print(result, spam)
options: None ['cat', 'dog', 'moose']
['cat', 'dog', 'moose'] ['cat', 'dog', 'moose']
None ['cat', 'dog']
moose ['cat', 'dog', 'moose']
why: append() changes spam and returns None, which is what result holds.

q: In spam.insert(1, 'x'), what does the 1 mean?
options: The number of copies of the item to insert
The index of the item that the new one replaces
The index where the new item goes
The new item goes after the item at index 1
why: insert(index, value) puts the value at that index and moves the later items along.

q: What does this program print?
code:
spam = ['cat', 'dog', 'bat']
spam.insert(1, 'chicken')
spam.insert(len(spam), 'end')
print(spam)
options: ['cat', 'dog', 'chicken', 'bat', 'end']
['chicken', 'cat', 'dog', 'bat', 'end']
['cat', 'chicken', 'dog', 'bat', 'end']
['cat', 'chicken', 'bat', 'end']
why: insert(1, ...) puts 'chicken' before 'dog', and insert(len(spam), ...) has the same effect as append.

q: What happens when spam[1] = 'x' is run on a list of four items?
options: 'x' is inserted at index 1 and the list gets five items
The item at index 1 is replaced, the length stays four
A new list is made and spam keeps the old one
IndexError, because index 1 already holds a value
why: Assigning to an index replaces the item there in the same list.

q: What does this program print?
code:
spam = ['cat', 'bat', 'rat', 'elephant']
spam[1] = 'aardvark'
spam[2] = spam[1]
spam[-1] = 12345
print(spam)
options: ['cat', 'aardvark', 'aardvark', 12345]
['cat', 'aardvark', 'rat', 12345]
['cat', 'aardvark', 'bat', 12345]
['cat', 'aardvark', 'aardvark', 'elephant', 12345]
why: Each statement sees the list as the previous one left it: spam[2] copies the new 'aardvark' and the negative index replaces the last item.

q: What does letters[1:3] = [] do to a list?
options: It empties the whole list, as letters[:] = [] does
It raises TypeError, because a slice cannot be assigned to
It replaces the two items with None and keeps the length
It deletes the items at indexes 1 and 2
why: Assigning a list to a slice replaces those items and may change the length, so assigning an empty list deletes them.

q: Which way of removing an item from a list also gives that item back?
options: remove()
del
pop()
clear()
why: pop() removes an item and returns it; remove() and clear() return None and del is a statement that gives back nothing.

q: A list holds three items equal to 'cat'. What does spam.remove('cat') do?
options: It deletes all three
It deletes only the first of them
It deletes the last of them
It deletes the first one and returns it
why: remove() deletes only the first match and returns None.

q: What does this program print?
options: missing ['bat', 'hat']
missing ['cat', 'bat', 'cat', 'hat']
missing ['cat', 'bat', 'hat']
missing ['bat', 'cat', 'hat']
why: The first 'cat' goes, the second stays, and removing a missing value raises ValueError, which the except clause handles.

q: What does pop(0) do to a list?
options: It removes the first item and returns it
It removes the item whose value is 0
It removes the last item and returns it
It returns the first item and leaves it in the list
why: pop() with an index removes the item at that index and returns it; without an argument it takes the last item.

q: What does this program print?
code:
nums = [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
a = nums.pop()
b = nums.pop(0)
print(a, b, nums)
why: pop() takes 7 from the end and pop(0) takes 3 from the front, leaving the three middle items.

q: How does del spam[2] differ from spam.pop(2)?
options: del leaves a gap that holds None at index 2
del removes the value 2 while pop() removes the index 2
Both remove it, but only pop() gives it back
del makes a new list while pop() changes the old one
why: The later items move up one index after either, and unlike pop() the del statement returns nothing.

q: What does this program print?
code:
spam = ['cat', 'bat', 'rat', 'elephant']
del spam[2]
del spam[2]
print(spam)
options: ['cat', 'bat', 'elephant']
['cat', 'bat']
['cat', 'elephant']
['cat', 'bat', 'rat']
why: After the first del the later items move up, so index 2 holds 'elephant' and the second del removes that.

q: Which of these gives a new list and leaves the original list as it was?
options: A slice such as spam[1:3]
spam.sort(), which orders spam
spam.reverse(), which turns spam round
spam.append(1), which adds an item
why: Slices, the + operator and comprehensions give new lists, while sort(), reverse() and append() change the list they are called on.

q: What does the * operator do when one side is a list and the other an integer?
options: It multiplies every item by the integer
It raises TypeError, since a list cannot be multiplied
It repeats the items inside the same list
It repeats the items and gives a new list
why: The + and * operators build new lists from old ones; * repeats the items and changes neither operand.

q: What happens to the operands in [1, 2] + [3]?
options: The left list is extended in place
The right list is appended to the left one, which changes both
Neither changes, and a new list is made
Python adds the numbers and gives [6]
why: Each of + and * makes a new list and changes neither operand.

q: What does this program print?
code:
a = [1, 2]
b = a + [3]
c = a * 2
print(a, b, c)
why: + joins two lists and * repeats the items, and a stays as it was because both make new lists.

q: After b = a and then a += [2], why does b show the new item too?
options: += extends the same list in place, and b names that list too
+= copies the list into b as well
b = a made b a separate copy that += then updates
+= is the same as a = a + [2], which changes both names
why: For a list the augmented operation is done in place, so every name for that list sees the change.

q: What does this program print?
code:
a = [1]
b = a
a += [2]
c = a
a = a + [3]
print(b, c, a)
why: += changes the one list that a, b and c share, and the last line binds a to a new list.

q: What does the in operator tell you about a list?
options: Whether an item of the list equals the value, as True or False
The index at which the value is found, or -1 if it is absent
Whether the value is itself a list or not
How many times the value occurs in the list
why: in and not in test whether a value is an item of the list and give a Boolean, while index() gives the position.

q: Why is 'gg' in 'eggs' True while 'gg' in ['eggs'] is False?
options: Lists are searched case-sensitively and strings are not
On a string in looks for a substring, on a list for an equal item
'gg' is not a valid item for a list, so it is skipped
in only looks at the first item of a list, not the rest
why: The operator tests for a substring on a string and for an equal item on a list.

q: What does this program print?
code:
pets = ['cat', 'dog']
print('dog' in pets, 'do' in pets, 'do' in 'dog', 'cat' not in pets)
options: True True True False
True False False False
True False True False
True False True True
why: 'do' is not an item of the list but is a substring of the string, and not in gives the opposite of in.

q: What does spam.index('Pooka') return when 'Pooka' occurs twice in the list?
options: The index of the first one
A list of both indexes
The index of the last one
How many times it occurs
why: index() returns the position of the first match, and a start argument finds a later one.

q: What does this program print?
options: 1 3 None
why: The first 'Pooka' is at 1, the search from index 2 finds the one at 3, and a missing value raises ValueError.

q: Why can len(spam) > 0 and spam[0] == 'cat' run on an empty list without an error?
options: Indexing an empty list gives None
The right side is evaluated before the left side
and skips the right side when the left side is false
Python catches the IndexError silently
why: and does not evaluate its right side when the left is false, so the index is never tried.

q: What does this program print?
code:
spam = []
print(len(spam) > 0 and spam[0] == 'cat', [] and 'x', 'x' or 1 / 0)
options: IndexError
False [] x
False False x
False [] True
why: The first test stops at False, and and and or return the operand that decided the result and not a Boolean.

q: Which pair of list methods reorders the list itself, in place?
options: sorted() and reversed()
sort() and reverse()
sort() and sorted()
sorted() and reverse()
why: sort() and reverse() reorder a list in place, while sorted() gives a reordered copy.

q: Why does spam = spam.sort() leave spam as None?
options: sort() only works on copies of a list, never on the list itself
sort() returns True or False to say whether it sorted
sort() works in place and returns None, which replaces the list
Sorting a list always gives None, whatever the items are
why: A method that changes a mutable object returns None, so the assignment overwrites the sorted list with None.

q: What does this program print?
code:
spam = [2, 5, 3.14, 1, -7]
result = spam.sort()
print(result, spam)
why: sort() reorders spam in place and returns None; integers and floats compare with each other.

q: What does key=str.lower change about sort()?
options: The items are compared as lowercase text but stay unchanged
The items are converted to lowercase inside the list itself
Items written in uppercase are removed before the sort
The sort becomes descending instead of ascending
why: The key function is called once for each item and only decides the order.

q: What does this program print?
code:
words = ['a', 'z', 'A', 'Z']
words.sort(key=str.lower)
print(words)
why: Compared as lowercase, 'a' and 'A' tie and so do 'z' and 'Z', and items with equal keys keep their original order.

q: How does [1, 2, 3][::-1] differ from calling reverse() on a list?
options: The slice gives a reversed copy; reverse() works in place
The slice changes the list in place; reverse() gives a copy
Both change the list in place and return the list
Both give a reversed copy and keep the original list
why: reverse() works in place and returns None, and the slice gives a reversed copy.

q: What does this program print?
code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a[::-1]
c = a.reverse()
print(a, b, c)
why: The slice made b as a reversed copy, then reverse() reversed a itself and returned None.

q: Which statement about sorted(spam) is true?
options: It sorts spam in place and returns None
It works only on lists
It returns a new list; spam stays as it was
It returns a sorted tuple
why: sorted() returns a new sorted list from any iterable and leaves the original alone.

q: What does this program print?
code:
data = [('red', 1), ('blue', 1), ('red', 2), ('blue', 2)]
print(sorted(data, key=lambda p: p[0]))
why: Sorting is stable, so items with equal keys keep their original order: ('blue', 1) stays before ('blue', 2).

q: You need the scores both in their original order and sorted. Which is the right approach?
options: scores = scores.sort() and keep scores
ordered = sorted(scores), and keep scores
scores.sort() and then scores.reverse()
ordered = scores and then ordered.sort()
why: sorted() gives a new list, while the other choices sort the only list there is, lose it to None, or sort a second name for the same list.

q: Which two techniques does the chapter use to take a list apart into its items?
options: A slice and the in operator together
The append and pop methods together
A for loop and a multiple assignment
The sort and reverse methods together
why: A for loop and a multiple assignment are the two ways the chapter takes a list apart.

q: When is enumerate() a better choice than range(len(spam))?
options: When the loop needs each item and its position, without indexing
When the list has to be changed while the loop runs
When the loop has to run faster than any other kind of loop
When the list is empty and nothing should run
why: enumerate() returns the index and the item on each pass, so the list does not have to be indexed.

q: What values does i take in for i in range(len(supplies)) when supplies holds four items?
options: The four items themselves
why: range(len(supplies)) visits the indexes 0 to 3.

q: What does this program print?
code:
supplies = ['pens', 'staplers', 'flamethrowers', 'binders']
total = 0
for i in range(len(supplies)):
    total += i
    i = 10
print(total, i)
why: Assigning to i does not change which index comes next, so total is 0+1+2+3, and the name i still exists after the loop.

q: What does enumerate(spam, start=1) change?
options: The first item is skipped by the loop
The list itself is renumbered from 1
The counter starts at 1; the items stay
The loop runs one time fewer than before
why: enumerate() returns a counter and an item on each pass, and start sets where the counter begins.

q: What does this program print?
code:
pairs = [(n, item) for n, item in enumerate(['pens', 'staplers'], start=1)]
print(pairs)
options: [(0, 'pens'), (1, 'staplers')]
[(1, 'pens'), (2, 'staplers')]
[(1, 'staplers')]
[('pens', 1), ('staplers', 2)]
why: Each pass gives the counter first and the item second, counting from 1.

q: Why does removing items from a list while a for loop runs over it skip items?
options: remove() ends the loop early, before the last item is reached
Python copies the list when the loop starts
A for loop visits only every second item after a change
The loop counts positions, so the next item slides into a passed place
why: The iterator counts positions, so after a removal the next item slides into the place just visited.

q: What does this program print?
why: Removing 1 moves 2 into position 0, which the loop has already passed, so 2 is never tested.

q: A loop must remove every item below 3 from items and skip none. Which change fixes it?
options: Call items.sort() before the loop
Loop over items.copy() while removing from items
Use del items[x] instead of items.remove(x)
Use items.pop() instead of items.remove(x)
why: Looping over a copy keeps the positions steady while the original list loses its items; the other changes still shift positions or use the values as indexes.

q: What does [x for x in vec if x >= 0] build?
options: It removes the negative items from vec itself
A list of True and False values
A new list of the items that are not negative
A generator that has not run yet
why: A list comprehension builds a new list and does not change the list it reads.

q: What does this program print?
code:
vec = [-4, -2, 0, 2, 4]
squares = [x ** 2 for x in vec if x >= 0]
print(squares, len(vec))
why: Only 0, 2 and 4 pass the test and are squared, and vec keeps its five items.

q: What must hold for a plain multiple assignment such as a, b, c = spam to work?
options: spam must be a list and not a tuple
spam must hold at least three items
The names must be in alphabetical order
spam must hold exactly three items
why: Without a starred target the number of names must equal the number of items, or Python raises ValueError.

q: How does a, b = b, a swap two values?
options: Both names get the value of b, because a is assigned first
It only works for numbers, since only they can be swapped
The right side is packed into a tuple, then unpacked into a and b
Python keeps a hidden list of all variables and swaps inside it
why: Multiple assignment is a combination of tuple packing and sequence unpacking, so the right side is fully evaluated first.

q: What does this program print?
code:
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a + b
print(a, b)
why: The right side becomes (2, 3) before either name changes, so a + b uses the old a.

q: What does the starred name collect in head, *middle, last = range(5)?
options: Every item, including the first and the last, as a tuple
Only the last item
Nothing, because it is a syntax error
The items between the first and the last, as a list
why: A starred target collects the remaining items into a list.

q: What does this program print?
code:
first, *rest = ['fat', 'gray', 'loud']
head, *middle, last = range(5)
print(first, rest, middle, last)
options: fat ('gray', 'loud') [1, 2, 3] 4
fat ['gray', 'loud'] [1, 2, 3] 4
fat ['gray', 'loud'] (1, 2, 3) 4
why: The starred names always receive a list, and the plain names take the first and the last items.

q: What do lists, strings, tuples and range objects have in common?
options: They are all mutable sequences that can be changed in place
They can all be changed by assigning to an item
They are sequences, so indexing, len() and in work on them all
They all hold only text and nothing else
why: Lists, strings and tuples share the sequence operations; only the list, of these, can be changed in place.

q: Among list, str, tuple and range, which is the only mutable sequence type?
options: list
str
tuple
range
why: Strings, tuples and range objects are immutable, and among the four only list is a mutable sequence.

q: Why does name[7] = 'the' raise TypeError when name is a string?
options: Index 7 is out of range for that string
A string is immutable, so items cannot be assigned
Strings can only hold letters and never words
'the' is longer than one character
why: Strings and tuples are immutable, and a changed string has to be built from slices.

q: What does this program print?
code:
name = 'Zophie a cat'
new = name[0:7] + 'the' + name[8:12]
try:
    name[0] = 'z'
    flag = 'changed'
except TypeError:
    flag = 'immutable'
print(new, flag, name)
options: Zophie the cat immutable Zophie a cat
Zophie the cat changed zophie a cat
Zophie the cat immutable Zophie the cat
Zophie a cat immutable Zophie a cat
why: The new string is built from slices, the item assignment fails, and the original string is untouched.

q: How does Python read ('hello') compared with ('hello',)?
options: Both are tuples, since brackets make a tuple
Both are strings, since the comma is ignored
The first is a tuple, the second is a syntax error
The first is a string, the second a one-item tuple
why: The comma makes the tuple, and brackets alone only group.

q: What does this program print?
code:
t = (['foo'], 'bar')
t[0].append('item')
print(t, type(('hello')).__name__)
options: (['foo'], 'bar') str
(['foo', 'item'], 'bar') tuple
(['foo', 'item'], 'bar') str
TypeError
why: An immutable tuple can hold a mutable list, which append() can change, and ('hello') is only a string.

q: What does a variable that was assigned a list actually hold?
options: A copy of every item of the list
The name of the list
A reference to the list object
The number of items of the list
why: A variable holds a reference, and that decides what assignment, a function call and a copy do to a list.

q: After spam = [0, 1, 2] and eggs = spam, why does eggs[1] = 'x' show in spam?
options: Assignment copied no list, so both names refer to one list
Python copies lists lazily and has not copied yet
Assigning to an item changes every list of the same length
eggs is a live view onto a slice of spam
why: Assignment binds a name to an object and copies nothing.

q: What does this program print?
code:
spam = 42
eggs = spam
spam = 99
a = [0, 1, 2, 3]
b = a
b[1] = 'Hello!'
print(eggs, a, a is b)
options: 42 [0, 'Hello!', 2, 3] True
99 [0, 'Hello!', 2, 3] True
why: Rebinding spam does not touch eggs, but a and b are the same list, so the item change shows in both.

q: Why does items.append(1) inside a function change the caller's list, while items = items + [1] does not?
options: Lists are copied when they are passed to a function
append() is the only method allowed to change an argument
A function can change a list only by returning a new one
The parameter names the caller's list; + builds a new one
why: Arguments are passed by assignment: the function gets a reference, and rebinding a local name does not affect the caller.

q: What does this program print?
code:
def add_one(items):
    items.append(1)

def add_two(items):
    items = items + [2]
    return items

spam = [0]
add_one(spam)
add_two(spam)
print(spam)
why: add_one changes the list it received, while add_two builds a new list that nobody keeps.

q: A function receives a list and must not change the caller's list. Which design is safest?
options: Change a copy of the list inside the function
Assign items = items at the top of the function
Call items.sort() and return items
Document that callers must not pass a list
why: Arguments are references, so only working on a copy keeps the caller's list from changing.

q: Why do all three rows change after lists = [[]] * 3 and lists[0].append(3)?
options: append() works on every list at once
* copies the outer list but not the numbers
The three rows are references to one inner list
The rows are copies that Python keeps synchronised
why: Replicating a list with * repeats references to the same item.

q: What does this program print?
code:
a = [[None] * 2] * 3
b = [[None] * 2 for _ in range(3)]
a[0][0] = 5
b[0][0] = 5
print(a, b)
options: [[5, None], [None, None], [None, None]] [[5, None], [5, None], [5, None]]
[[5, None], [5, None], [5, None]] [[5, None], [None, None], [None, None]]
[[5, None], [None, None], [None, None]] [[5, None], [None, None], [None, None]]
[[5, None], [5, None], [5, None]] [[5, None], [5, None], [5, None]]
why: The product holds three references to one row, while the comprehension makes a new row on each pass.

q: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy of a list?
options: A shallow copy copies only the first item of the list
A shallow copy shares inner objects; a deep copy does not
A deep copy copies the name, a shallow copy the value
A shallow copy is read-only and cannot be changed later
why: A shallow copy holds references to the same items, while copy.deepcopy() copies the inner lists as well.

q: Which expression gives a new list that shares its items with spam, a shallow copy?
options: eggs = spam
spam += []
spam[:]
copy.deepcopy(spam)
why: A slice, list.copy(), list() and copy.copy() make shallow copies, while assignment only adds a name.

q: What does this program print?
code:
import copy
a = [[1, 2], [3]]
b = copy.copy(a)
b[0].append('x')
b.append([4])
print(a, len(b))
why: The outer list b is new, so appending to it leaves a alone, but the inner list is shared.

q: When is copy.deepcopy() needed instead of copy.copy()?
options: When the inner lists must change independently
When the list holds only numbers and strings
When the list is empty and will be filled later
When the copy has to be sorted afterwards
why: A deep copy copies the inner lists as well, so changes to them do not show in the original.

q: What does this program print?
code:
import copy
nested = [[1, 2], [3]]
shallow = copy.copy(nested)
deep = copy.deepcopy(nested)
nested[0].append('changed')
print(shallow, deep)
why: The shallow copy shares the inner list and shows the change, and the deep copy does not.

q: Each player is a list [name, score] and players is a list of players. Which snapshot does not change when a score later changes?
options: players.copy(), which copies the outer list
copy.deepcopy(players)
players[:], which slices the whole list
list(players), which builds a list of it
why: The other three are shallow copies that share the inner player lists, so a changed score shows in them.

q: What do the chapter's random functions choice() and shuffle() take as the thing they work on?
options: A range of numbers only
A dictionary of weights
A list of items
A seed and a count
why: random.choice() and random.shuffle() take a list, the first to pick an item and the second to reorder it.

q: How do random.choice() and random.shuffle() differ in what they do to the list?
options: choice() leaves the list alone, shuffle() reorders it in place
choice() removes the item it returns, shuffle() returns a new list
Both return a new list
Both reorder the list in place
why: choice() does not change the list, while shuffle() reorders it in place and returns None.

q: What does random.choice([]) do?
options: It raises IndexError
It returns None
It returns []
It returns 0
why: random.choice() raises IndexError for an empty sequence.

q: What does this program print? The picks are random, but 50 of them always come from the list.
code:
import random
pets = ['Dog', 'Cat', 'Moose']
picks = [random.choice(pets) for _ in range(50)]
print(all(p in pets for p in picks), len(pets))
options: False 3
True 2
True 50
True 3
why: choice() returns an item of the list and does not change the list, so it still holds three items.

q: What does random.shuffle(people) return?
options: A new shuffled list
None, after reordering people in place
The shuffled list and the original list
One random item of the list
why: shuffle() reorders the list in place and returns None; sample(x, k=len(x)) gives a shuffled new list.

q: What does this program print? The order after the shuffle is random, but the sorted list is not.
code:
import random
people = ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'David']
result = random.shuffle(people)
print(result, sorted(people))
options: ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'David'] None
None []
None ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'David']
None ['David', 'Carol', 'Bob', 'Alice']
why: shuffle() returns None and keeps the same four items, so sorting them gives the original alphabetical order.

q: What does the Magic 8 Ball program keep in a list?
options: The questions the person has typed so far
The random numbers it has drawn so far
The possible answers, one picked by an index
The characters of the screen
why: The program stores its nine answers in the list messages and picks one by a random index.

q: Why does messages[random.randint(0, len(messages) - 1)] subtract 1 from the length?
options: randint includes both ends, and the last index is len minus 1
randint excludes its upper end, so the 1 makes up for it
The first answer must never be picked, so the range is cut
len() returns one too many for every list of answers
why: randint(a, b) can return b, so b has to be the last valid index, len(messages) - 1.

q: What does this program print? The draws are random, but 500 draws from four values leave no value out.
why: randint includes both ends, so 0 and 3 both occur, 4 never does, and 500 draws see every value.

q: What does each counter in columns = [0] * WIDTH stand for in the Matrix Screensaver?
options: The character that is printed in that column
A pause in seconds for that row of the screen
A random number shared by the whole screen
How many more characters its column will print
why: A counter above zero prints a random character and counts down, and a zero prints a space.

q: What does this program print?
code:
WIDTH = 5
columns = [0] * WIDTH
columns[2] = 3
row = ''
for i in range(WIDTH):
    if columns[i] > 0:
        row += '#'
        columns[i] -= 1
    else:
        row += '.'
print(repr(row), columns)
why: Only the column with a positive counter prints a character and counts down; a decrement placed outside that branch would push the zeros below zero.

q: In the function that turns a list into 'apples, bananas, tofu, and cats', why is the last item handled apart from the others?
options: The last item has a different type from the others
join() cannot join more than three items at once
Only the last item gets 'and' in front of it
A list cannot be joined with commas at all
why: The items before the last are joined with ', ' and the last one gets ', and ' in front of it.

q: What does this program print?
options: 'apples, bananas, tofu, and cats' '' 'apples'
'apples, bananas, tofu, cats' '' 'apples'
'apples, bananas, tofu, and cats' '' ', and apples'
'apples, bananas, and tofu, cats' '' 'apples'
